studies.answer: Mostly the car, and more than ever. Today about 90% of the gap between drivers' results lines up with the team they drive for, against 44% in the 1950s.
studies.intro: Every fan argument ends up here. Would a great driver win in a slow car, and would an average one win in the best car? The archive can't settle it for any one driver, but across 75 years of results it shows clearly how much the car has come to decide.
studies.method: Results from every championship race since 1950, without the Indianapolis 500 that counted until 1960. A regular driver started at least half of a season's races. The best car is the team with the most points that season. Teammate records count every pair of cars from the same team in a race, so the 1950s, when teams ran four or five cars, give more chances per race.

chart.title: Share of the spread in results that lines up with the team

parts.text: For each season we take every regular driver's average finishing place and ask how much of the spread between them disappears once you know their team. If teammates always finished side by side it would be 100%. It has climbed almost every decade, as cars became harder to build, teams fewer and better funded, and the gap between the best and worst car grew.

chart.title: Seasons where the champion drove for the top scoring team

parts.text: In 58 of 76 finished seasons the champion drove for the team that scored the most points that year. The exceptions are the famous ones, like Räikkönen in 2007, Hamilton in 2008, Verstappen in 2021, Verstappen in 2024. Even then the car was close: in 14 of those 18 seasons the champion's team was second, and the lowest was Keke Rosberg's Williams in 1982, fourth.

chart.title: Finished ahead of the teammate, both cars classified (100+ races)

parts.text: The part the car doesn't explain is the one fans care about. The fairest test is the teammate, same car, same day. Counting only races where both cars finished, so breakdowns don't count, Max Verstappen has finished ahead of his teammate in 84% of 183 chances, the best record of anyone with 100 or more.

studies.title: Car or driver?

studies.answer: Cars used to break all the time. In the 1980s only 47% of starters saw the flag, now it's 87%, and races got more predictable because of it.
studies.intro: Retirements used to be part of the show. A leader's engine could let go with three laps left and hand the win to someone nobody expected. That has almost gone, and it changed how races are won.
studies.method: Every championship race since 1950, without the Indianapolis 500 that counted until 1960. Starters leave out cars that withdrew or didn't start. A car is counted as broken for any mechanical cause (engine, gearbox, brakes and so on), a crash covers accidents, collisions, spins and damage. Drivers running at the end but too far behind to be classified count as not finishing. Top three teams are by points that season, finished seasons only.

parts.h: Who makes it to the flag
parts.text: Until 2000 about half the field finished. The low point was the 1980s, with turbo engines, tiny fuel limits and 26 car grids. Things turned in the 2000s, when engines had to last more than one race weekend and teams got far better at testing parts before races.

chart.title: Share of starts that ended early

parts.text: At worst a driver had a 39% chance of their car breaking in any race, about two races in five. By the early 2020s it was 6%. Crashes went the other way for a while, peaking in the 1990s, and are now about as common as breakdowns, so a modern retirement is as likely to be the driver's fault as the car's. From 2023 the official records just say "Retired" without a reason, so the table stops there.

chart.title: Wins for a team outside that season's top three

parts.text: When cars broke, the fast teams lost wins they deserved. In the 1980s 18% of races went to a team outside that season's top three. With cars that never fail, the best car nearly always gets its result, which is a big part of why the order feels so fixed now.

studies.title: The death of the DNF
